Operator: Good day, and welcome to the NovaTel Media Q3 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. Instructions for queuing your questions will be provided at that time. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to NovaTel Media's Q3 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me on the call today are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Patel, Chief Network Officer; David Kim, Chief Commercial Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more complete discussion of these risks.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I am excited to share our Q3 results, which reflect our commitment to innovation and customer satisfaction. We achieved strong performance across several key areas.

First, our spectrum assets utilization exceeded expectations, with efficient deployment driving capacity gains. Second, we continue to see strong adoption of our 5G fixed wireless access services, leading to meaningful ARPU uplift. Third, our focus on service revenue growth across wireless, broadband, and enterprise has yielded impressive results. Fourth, we are making significant strides in managing cost of revenue trends. Fifth, our efforts in net subscriber additions by residential and business segments are paying off handsomely. Sixth, we are strategically optimizing subscriber acquisition costs, and finally, we are exploring advanced network slicing for media applications.

Michael Chen: Thank you, Sarah. Now, let's move on to the financial results. Our revenue for the quarter reached $16.5 billion, an increase of 8% compared to the same period last year. Adjusted EBITDA was $3.8 billion, resulting in a margin of 38%. We are diligently managing our costs and optimizing our capital allocation. Capital expenditures amounted to $1.2 billion, primarily allocated to 5G infrastructure, fiber deployment, and content acquisition.

As we dive deeper into the details of our Q3 results, I want to spend some time on one of our most critical strategic assets: our spectrum portfolio. In the hyper-competitive telecom and media landscape, spectrum is the lifeblood of our wireless operations, enabling everything from high-speed 5G broadband to low-latency media delivery for streaming services like our partnerships with Peacock and Disney+. Today, I'll break down our current utilization rates, key trends driving demand, regional nuances, technical initiatives underway, and our forward-looking allocation plans. We've made tremendous progress here, positioning us to capture the explosive growth in data consumption—now averaging 25 GB per month per postpaid subscriber, up 18% year-over-year, fueled by 4K/8K video streaming, cloud gaming, and IoT deployments.

Let's start with the numbers. As of Q3 end, our total mid-band spectrum holdings stand at approximately 320 MHz on average across our top 100 markets, including our prized 160 MHz of C-band (3.7-3.98 GHz) acquired in the FCC's Auction 110 for $9.2 billion, and 110 MHz of premium 2.5 GHz BRS/EBS spectrum refarmed from legacy video services. Low-band assets, like our 20 MHz nationwide at 600 MHz, provide wide coverage, while mmWave—about 1.2 GHz in select urban footprints—handles ultra-high-capacity needs.

Utilization is strong and efficient: overall network spectral efficiency has improved to 4.2 bits/Hz, up from 3.1 bits/Hz a year ago, thanks to massive MIMO and 256-QAM modulation. Average utilization sits at 72% during peak hours (7-11 PM), with urban core markets like New York, LA, and Chicago hitting 85-90% loads driven by media-heavy usage—think NFL Sunday Ticket streams and live concert AR experiences. Rural and suburban areas hover at 55-65%, giving us ample headroom. Year-over-year, peak throughput has surged 45% to 850 Mbps median on 5G SA devices, outpacing T-Mobile's reported 750 Mbps and closing the gap with Verizon's fiber-backed mmWave deployments.

Traffic trends underscore the urgency: wireless data usage grew 32% YoY, with video accounting for 65% of that—mirroring industry shifts as cord-cutting accelerates. Our fixed wireless access (FWA) service, leveraging C-band, now serves 1.2 million households at 300 Mbps symmetrical speeds, contributing $180 million in incremental revenue, with take rates up 15 points to 28% in eligible markets.

Performance varies by footprint, reflecting tailored strategies. In the Northeast and California metros—our densest 20 markets covering 120 million POPs—we're at 82% utilization, constrained by high media demand from events like Coachella broadcasts and Broadway VR pilots. Here, we're prioritizing carrier aggregation combos like n41 (2.5 GHz) + n77 (C-band) to deliver 1.2 Gbps peaks.

The Midwest and Southeast, with 85 million POPs, show 68% utilization, benefiting from lower population density but rising IoT from precision ag partnerships with John Deere. Sunbelt markets like Texas and Florida are the growth engines at 75% utilization, up 12 points YoY, as snowbirds drive seasonal FWA adoption—ARPU uplift of $8 per user from bundled media packs.

Internationally, our joint venture with Vodafone in Europe utilizes 140 MHz mid-band across the UK and Germany, at 70% load, supporting 5G Open RAN trials for cost-efficient media edge caching.

We're not resting on our laurels. Key initiatives include dynamic spectrum sharing (DSS) rolled out across 80% of our 2.5 GHz footprint, allowing seamless 4G/5G coexistence and boosting utilization by 15% without service disruption—critical as we sunset 3G by Q4 2025, refarming 30 MHz for 5G NR. Network slicing for media, in partnership with Ericsson, deploys end-to-end slices on C-band for ultra-reliable low-latency comms (URLLC), targeting <5ms for live sports streaming and metaverse events. Early pilots with NBA teams show 99.999% reliability. CBRS private networks, leveraging 150 MHz in the 3.5 GHz band for enterprise media clients like Netflix studios, with 200 deployments live, generating $50 million in new recurring revenue. Our proprietary RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) dynamically allocates spectrum, reducing interference by 22% and improving efficiency in contested mmWave bands against rivals like Starlink's fixed satellite push.

These efforts have delivered a 28% YoY increase in MHz-POPs coverage, from 2.1 trillion to 2.7 trillion, enhancing our competitive moat.

Looking ahead, we're laser-focused on reallocating spectrum for maximum ROI amid the 5G-Advanced ramp-up. CapEx for spectrum-related initiatives will total $4.5 billion in FY24, flat YoY, with 60% directed to C-band expansion: full buildout of our 160 MHz by YE25, prioritizing 100 million new POPs in mid-sized markets. This mid-band "goldilocks" spectrum—propagation sweet spot for coverage and capacity—will drive 5G SA penetration from 45% to 75%, unlocking $2-3 ARPU uplift via premium media tiers. Refarming legacy holdings by sunsetting 700 MHz legacy voice by mid-2025, reallocating 40 MHz to n71 for extended rural FWA, targeting 3 million new subs and competing head-on with T-Mobile's 2.5 GHz hoard. Auction participation eyes FCC's 3.45-3.55 GHz DoD spectrum release (up to 100 MHz) and mmWave Auction 112, with $3 billion dry powder. In Europe, bidding for harmonized 26 GHz with EU partners. Spectrum leasing and sharing includes new deals with Dish Network for 40 MHz CBRS reciprocity and potential AWS-3 swaps, optimizing our portfolio without auctions.

Strategically, this positions us for the media convergence wave: 5G will power 40% of our video traffic by 2027, enabling monetization through network-as-a-service for hyperscalers like AWS and edge computing for Hollywood VFX rendering. Risks include regulatory delays—FCC auction timelines slipped 6 months last year—and competitive intensity, but our 3.1x leverage ratio gives flexibility. We expect spectrum-driven EBITDA margins to expand 200 bps to 48% by FY26.

Before moving to other metrics, I'd like to address our balance sheet strength, particularly our debt levels and leverage ratios, as this remains a key focus for investors given the capital-intensive nature of our telecom and media operations. We continue to execute on our deleveraging strategy amid a favorable macro environment, including the Fed's recent rate cuts, which have supported our refinancing activities.

As of September 30th, our gross debt stood at $48.2 billion, comprising $22 billion in senior unsecured notes, $15 billion in term loans, $8 billion in secured facilities primarily backed by our U.S. wireless spectrum assets, and $3.2 billion in short-term commercial paper. After netting $4.1 billion in cash and short-term investments—bolstered by our $1.8 billion in Q3 free cash flow generation—our net debt is $44.1 billion. This reflects a modest $500 million reduction quarter-over-quarter, driven by $1.2 billion in debt repayments funded by operational cash flows and proceeds from non-core tower monetizations.

Turning to our headline leverage metric, our net debt to last twelve months (LTM) adjusted EBITDA ratio came in at 3.6x for the quarter, down 20 basis points from 3.8x at Q2 end and a full turn lower than the 4.6x we reported this time last year. For context, our adjusted EBITDA for the LTM period was $12.3 billion, up 8% year-over-year, fueled by 5% wireless service revenue growth in North America—where postpaid ARPU expanded 3.2% to $58.40 on 5G Ultra Wideband adoption now at 65% of our subscriber base—and a 12% ramp in our NovaStream SVOD platform, which added 2.1 million net adds to reach 45 million domestic subscribers.

This deleveraging trajectory puts us comfortably within our target range of 3.0x to 3.5x by year-end 2025, ahead of the Street's consensus. Compared to peers, we're now running leaner than AT&T's 3.9x and on par with Comcast's 3.5x, while trading at a discount to Verizon's 3.2x on an EV/EBITDA multiple basis. In Europe, where we've been pruning our legacy 3G/4G footprint, our regional leverage sits even lower at 2.8x, benefiting from €1.5 billion in divestiture proceeds from our Spanish cable assets sold to a consortium led by Digi in Q2.

Key drivers of this improvement include several technical initiatives we've executed flawlessly. First, in July, we refinanced $6 billion of our 2026 term loan B at SOFR plus 175 basis points—a 100 bps tightening from the prior all-in rate of 5.9%—locking in $250 million in annual interest savings through 2028. This was complemented by a $4 billion senior notes issuance in the 5.25% coupon range for our 10-year tranche, taking advantage of the post-election yield curve steepening. We've also drawn just 15% on our $10 billion revolving credit facility, maintaining ample liquidity with $8.5 billion in total available capacity, including undrawn accordion features.

On the EBITDA side, our adjustments are standard for the industry: excluding one-offs like the $180 million integration costs from our 2023 Liberty Latin America acquisition and $120 million in spectrum lease amortization tied to our C-band holdings. Pro forma for the pending $2.8 billion acquisition of Mid-Atlantic FiberNet—which will add 3,000 route miles of dark fiber for enterprise edge computing—we still project leverage holding below 3.7x.

Regionally, North America remains our leverage anchor, with wireless capex moderating to 14% of service revenues as 5G Standalone (SA) core deployment hits 85% coverage, shifting spend toward Open RAN trials with Nokia and Ericsson to cut opex by 20% over five years. In APAC, where we're scaling our fixed wireless access (FWA) partnerships with Starlink for rural Indonesia, leverage is higher at 4.1x due to $900 million in recent 3.6 GHz spectrum auction wins, but offset by 25% EBITDA margins from high-ARPU enterprise services. Media-side investments in original content for NovaStream—including our $500 million commitment to AI-enhanced personalization tech akin to Netflix's playbook—are accretive, with content capex now just 7% of segment revenues.

Strategically, we're prioritizing three levers to accelerate deleveraging into 2025: one, sustained FCF generation targeting $5.5 billion annually, with 90% allocated to debt paydown and buybacks; two, non-core asset rotations like our planned 20% stake sale in NovaTowers REIT, potentially yielding $2 billion and mirroring Crown Castle's model; and three, M&A selectivity in fiber and content to boost consolidated EBITDA margins toward 42%, in line with Charter's trajectory.

We view our balance sheet as a competitive moat in this consolidating industry, positioning NovaTel Media to capitalize on 5G monetization, streaming bundling with telco services—think our 'NovaBundle' with 15% uptake—and the looming 6G spectrum pipeline. Risks like regulatory hurdles in Europe under the Digital Markets Act or U.S. net neutrality reinstatement are mitigated by our flexible capital structure, with no major maturities until 2027.

Next, let's turn to our service revenue performance, which grew 6.8% year-over-year to $14.2 billion, marking our ninth straight quarter of expansion and outperforming our guided range of 5-7%. This resilience underscores the strength of our converged telecom and media portfolio amid moderating inflation, spectrum auction dynamics, and intensifying competition from players like T-Mobile and Charter.

Starting with wireless service revenue, up 4.5% YoY to $8.9 billion. This was propelled by robust postpaid net adds of 1.2 million—our strongest quarter since Q1 2022—driven by our Ultra5G Unlimited plan, which bundles 5G Advanced with ad-supported Paramount+ and Peacock streaming tiers. ARPU climbed 2.8% to $52.40, fueled by premium pricing on family plans and device financing uptake amid the iPhone 16 cycle. Churn held steady at 0.92%, below industry averages reported by the CTIA, thanks to our AI-powered Network Intelligence platform, which uses predictive analytics to preempt service disruptions.

Regionally, U.S. wireless grew 5.2%, benefiting from our mid-band C-band spectrum deployment covering 85% of our footprint—on par with Verizon's progress—and fixed wireless access (FWA) trials adding 150,000 households in rural markets. In Europe, via our Vodafone joint venture, we saw 3.1% growth despite regulatory headwinds from the EU's Digital Markets Act, offset by Open RAN pilots in Spain reducing capex by 15%. Emerging markets like Latin America lagged at 2.7% due to FX volatility in Brazil and Argentina, but our prepaid 5G eSIM push is gaining traction with 20% MoM subscriber growth there.

Strategically, we're accelerating 5G Standalone (SA) core upgrades, enabling network slicing for low-latency gaming and AR/VR experiences in partnership with Epic Games. This positions us ahead of AT&T's curve and supports our 2025 target of 7-9% wireless growth.

Moving to broadband service revenue, which surged 8.2% YoY to $3.4 billion—our fastest-growing segment. Fiber-to-the-premises (FTTP) penetration hit 42% of our 35 million households passed, up from 35% a year ago, with 450,000 net adds from aggressive builds in the Sun Belt and Midwest. Average revenue per user (ARPU) rose 4.1% to $68.20, anchored by gigabit symmetrical speeds and bundles integrating our GlobalStream+ video service, which now boasts 12 million SVOD subs, rivaling Comcast's Xfinity Stream.

DOCSIS 4.0 upgrades in hybrid coax markets added 200,000 multi-gig subs, while FWA complemented fiber in underserved areas, capturing 15% market share per FCC broadband reports. U.S. growth was stellar at 9.1%, fueled by BEAD funding pursuits totaling $2.5 billion in grants; Europe delivered 6.8% via our Liberty Global merger synergies in the UK and Netherlands; and APAC contributed 4.5% through 5G home internet in India, despite Jio's pricing pressure.

Key insight: Our 'Fiber First' strategy, with $4.2 billion capex allocated this year, targets 50% FTTP penetration by 2026, de-risking us from cable cutters and positioning broadband as our cash flow engine for media investments.

Finally, enterprise service revenue increased 6.1% YoY to $2.0 billion, reflecting demand for our 5G Edge and private network solutions. Mobility services drove 4.8% growth with 250,000 net adds from SMBs adopting our Managed 5G WAN, while wireline and cloud-adjacent services grew 7.5% via SD-WAN and multi-access edge computing (MEC) deployments. Notable wins include a $500 million, 5-year deal with Ford for connected vehicle slicing and expansions with AWS for hybrid edge-cloud.

U.S. enterprise led at 7.2%, buoyed by hyperscaler ramps; EMEA grew 5.4% amid GDPR-compliant data sovereignty offerings; and we entered China via a Huawei-partnered private 5G network for manufacturing, adding 3.2% despite U.S. export controls. ARPU here expanded 3.6% to $1,450, with churn at 1.1%, below Gartner benchmarks.

Strategically, our Enterprise 5G Factory program—now live in 15 U.S. sites—leverages ORAN-compliant radios for customized slicing, giving us an edge over Ericsson-dependent rivals. We see enterprise accelerating to 8-10% growth in 2025 as Industry 4.0 adoption ramps.

In summary, service revenue's 6.8% growth reflects balanced execution across segments, with broadband and enterprise offsetting wireless normalization. Margins expanded 120 basis points to 48.5% on opex efficiencies from our GenAI operations center, which automates 30% of network tickets. Looking ahead, we reaffirm full-year service growth of 6-7% and raise 2025 guidance to 7-9%, contingent on spectrum wins in the ongoing FCC auction.

I'll now turn to our cost of revenue, where we continue to see disciplined management amid a dynamic industry landscape marked by aggressive 5G deployments, escalating content licensing battles, and fiber overbuild pressures. For the quarter, cost of revenue came in at $4.25 billion, up 7.2% year-over-year from $3.96 billion in Q2 2023, and up 2.1% sequentially from $4.16 billion in Q1 2024. As a percentage of revenue, this represents 52.3% of our top line, expanding 110 basis points YoY due to upfront investments in next-gen network capacity and competitive content acquisitions, partially offset by productivity gains from our NFV and automation initiatives.

Breaking this down by key components, network operations and interconnect costs hit $2.42 billion (57% of COR, +9.8% YoY). This is our largest bucket, driven primarily by mobile data traffic surging 28% YoY to 1.2 exabytes, fueled by 5G adoption now at 42% of our postpaid mobile base—up from 31% last year. Key drivers include 5G Standalone (SA) rollout: We've deployed SA core in 65% of our U.S. footprint, necessitating higher backhaul and edge computing opex. This added ~$180 million in incremental costs, akin to what we've seen at peers like T-Mobile during their mid-band 2.5 GHz expansion. Fiber expansion: In our broadband segment, FTTx passings grew 14% to 28 million homes, with associated leased dark fiber and maintenance costs up $95 million, pressured by rural overbuilds from rivals like Altice and Frontier. Interconnect and roaming: International roaming volumes jumped 22% amid summer travel recovery, adding $45 million, though we've mitigated this through bilateral agreements with European carriers like Vodafone.

Regionally, U.S. network costs rose 11% to $1.65 billion due to spectrum exhaustion in high-density markets like NYC and LA, where we're layering C-band assets acquired in the 2021 FCC auction. In Europe, costs were flat at €420 million equivalent, benefiting from Open RAN trials with Nokia that reduced vendor lock-in by 15%. Asia-Pacific saw a 5% uptick to A$220 million from Indonesia 5G greenfield builds.

Content acquisition and licensing reached $1.18 billion (28% of COR, +6.4% YoY). Our media arm continues to anchor bundles, with video subscribers stable at 18.5 million despite cord-cutting headwinds. Drivers here: Streaming wars escalation with linear and OTT content costs rose $75 million, including renewals for premium sports rights like NFL Sunday Ticket (mirroring Dish's $10B+ deal pain) and exclusive deals with Peacock for our Xfinity-like StreamTV bundle. SVOD wholesale fees from Netflix and Disney+ affiliates added $40 million as penetration hit 55% of our base. Original content amortization: $55 million tied to our in-house studio slate, including the hit series "Edgeworld," with production costs front-loaded for Q3 seasonality.

U.S. content spend dominated at 72% ($850 million), up on NBA and Premier League packages to combat YouTube TV poaching. Europe was more efficient at €180 million, leveraging EU content quotas for local originals that lowered reliance on Hollywood imports by 12%.

Customer premises equipment (CPE) and support: $442 million (10% of COR, -2.1% YoY). A bright spot, with declines driven by device mix shift: eSIM adoption at 35% reduced subsidized handset costs by $25 million; we're following Verizon's playbook with self-install kits cutting field ops by 18%. Wi-Fi 6E gateways: Bulk upgrades for 4 million broadband homes amortized to $120 million, but unit costs fell 14% via supply chain deals with Arris and Calix.

Despite topline growth, COR margins held resilient thanks to network function virtualization (NFV) and AI orchestration: Our cloud-native stack with Ericsson and AWS saved $120 million, or 5% of network opex, by dynamically scaling traffic—early wins from our Open RAN pilots mirroring AT&T's 20-30% capex savings trajectory. Zero-touch provisioning reduced support costs 8% via GenAI chatbots, handling 65% of Tier 1 queries. Strategic bundling: 5G + StreamTV ARPU uplift of $4.50/mo offset content inflation, with churn at a stellar 0.92%.

Looking regionally, U.S. COR intensity remains highest at 54% of revenue due to regulatory hurdles like the BEAD program's fiber subsidies favoring rivals. Europe benefits from lower spectrum costs post-3.6 GHz auctions, while APAC growth is tempered by MVNO partnerships with Singtel reducing capex leakage.

We expect Q4 COR at $4.35-$4.45 billion, implying 50-100 bps gross margin expansion as 5G traffic efficiencies kick in and content deals stabilize post-negotiations. Longer-term, our $18 billion 2024 capex plan—45% growth-focused—positions us for sub-50% COR/revenue by 2026, outpacing Comcast's trajectory through edge AI and wholesale 5G slicing to hyperscalers like AWS.

As we look at operational metrics, I'd like to focus on net subscriber additions by segment—residential and business—which remain a cornerstone of our growth strategy in this dynamic telecom and media landscape. For the quarter, we delivered total net subscriber additions of 178,000 RGUs across both segments, up 12% year-over-year and marking our eighth consecutive quarter of sequential growth. This performance underscores our execution on broadband expansion, 5G monetization, and bundled media offerings amid competitive pressures from players like Comcast, Charter, and T-Mobile's aggressive 5G fixed wireless push.

Residential continues to be our growth engine, with net adds of 152,000, a robust 18% YoY increase and accelerating from 128,000 in Q2. This was driven by a multi-pronged strategy leveraging our hybrid fiber-coax network and recent DOCSIS 4.0 upgrades, which now cover 65% of our footprint—putting us on par with Charter's Spectrum rollout.

Broadband led the way with +112,000 net adds, fueled by our 'Gigabit Everywhere' initiative. We added 45,000 FTTH subscribers in high-density markets like the Northeast Corridor (NYC metro and Boston), where penetration hit 28%—comparable to Verizon Fios levels. Fixed wireless access (FWA) via our 5G mmWave spectrum contributed another 32,000 adds in suburban Sun Belt regions like Atlanta and Dallas, where we're countering T-Mobile's 5G Home Internet with lower latency bundles at $50/month. Sequential broadband churn dipped to 1.1%, down from 1.3% last quarter, thanks to our AI-driven retention tools that proactively upsell speed tiers.

Video and mobile rounded it out: Postpaid mobile net adds of +25,000 reflected strong uptake of our MVNO partnership with Dish Network's Boost, bundling unlimited 5G with Netflix ad-supported tiers—a play mirroring Xfinity Mobile's success. Video RGUs grew by +15,000, bucking the cord-cutting trend (now at -2% industry-wide per Nielsen) through skinny bundles with Peacock and Paramount+ integrations, holding linear TV churn steady at 2.4%. Regionally, the Midwest saw 22% YoY growth in residential adds due to our $2B capex push into underserved rural pockets via the BEAD program, while California faced headwinds from regulatory pricing caps, limiting adds to +18,000.

ARPU in residential rose 3% QoQ to $128, reflecting premiumization—5G mobile ARPU now at $55, up from bundling synergies.

Our business segment posted 26,000 net adds, flat QoQ but up 5% YoY, as we navigate enterprise caution in a high-interest-rate environment. This segment's higher ARPU—averaging $450/month—makes it a profitability powerhouse, contributing 35% of service revenue despite lower volume.

SMBs drove +18,000 adds, with Ethernet and SD-WAN services surging 14% YoY. Our 'NexWave Business Fiber' product, now available to 75% of U.S. ZIP codes via dark fiber lit-up partnerships (similar to Lumen's enterprise strategy), resonated with retail and hospitality verticals. In the Southeast, adds hit +6,200 amid post-pandemic office returns, bolstered by cybersecurity bundles with Palo Alto Networks.

Enterprise added +8,000, focused on cloud on-ramps and edge computing. We secured 12 new Fortune 1000 contracts for 400G wavelength services, including a multi-year deal with a major media conglomerate for low-latency content delivery—think akin to AWS Direct Connect but optimized for 8K streaming. Churn here remained elite at 0.8%, thanks to our managed services platform, which integrates AI orchestration for 99.999% uptime SLAs. Internationally, our Latin America JV with Claro added +2,500 business RGUs in Mexico, capitalizing on nearshoring trends.

Strategic headwinds included elongated sales cycles in IT spending—down 10% industry-wide per IDC—but we're mitigating with 'pay-as-you-grow' models.

Overall, net adds trends signal resilience: residential broadband RGU growth outpaced the industry at 4.2% YoY (vs. 3.1% for cable peers), while business stabilized post-COVID volatility. Technically, our $1.8B Q3 capex—28% of revenue—funded 5G C-band densification (now 85% coverage) and PON overlays, positioning us for DOCSIS 4.0 symmetrical gigabit by mid-2024. Competitively, we're gaining share from satellite players like Starlink in rural broadband, with 15% lower CAC through digital self-install.

Looking forward, we guide to Q4 residential net adds of 165,000-175,000 and business at 25,000-30,000, assuming holiday bundling ramps and no major macro shocks. Our M&A pipeline, including bolt-on fiber assets in the Midwest, will further densify our network for 6-8% RGU growth in FY24. This subscriber momentum, paired with opex discipline, supports our raised FY24 EBITDA outlook.

Before we open it up to Q&A, I'd like to dive deeper into our subscriber acquisition cost—or SAC—trends, which have been a focal point for investors given the competitive dynamics in wireless, broadband, and our streaming vertical. SAC represents the fully loaded cost to onboard a new postpaid subscriber, including sales and marketing expenses, device subsidies, commissions, and promotional incentives, netted against any upfront payments. We report this on a per-subscriber basis across our segments.

In Q3, our blended SAC came in at $428 per postpaid net add, a 7% sequential decline from $461 in Q2 and a robust 12% year-over-year improvement from $486 in Q3 2022. This marks the fourth straight quarter of SAC moderation, reflecting the payoffs from our multi-year digital transformation and portfolio optimization efforts. For context, our wireless segment—which drove 62% of Q3 net adds—saw SAC dip to $512, down 9% QoQ and 15% YoY, while broadband SAC held steady at $287 (flat QoQ, -5% YoY), and our NovaStream direct-to-consumer platform achieved an industry-leading $112 SAC, a 14% YoY drop.

In wireless, SAC efficiency stems from three pillars. First, device subsidy rationalization: We've reduced average upfront subsidies by 18% YoY to $220 per smartphone line, prioritizing our own NovaFlex financing program—now at 45% penetration—over outright discounts. This mirrors T-Mobile's EIP success but with our proprietary AI underwriting, which has cut default rates to under 1.2%. Second, programmatic advertising ROI: Our $450 million Q3 marketing spend yielded a 3.2x return on ad spend (ROAS), up from 2.7x YoY, thanks to machine learning models targeting high-LTV prospects via Google DV360 and The Trade Desk. We've shifted 65% of acquisition media to CTV and DOOH, reducing CAC from search-heavy channels by 22%. Third, 5G Unlimited bundling: Promotions tying our 5G mmWave plans to NovaStream access boosted conversions by 28%, with ARPU uplift of $4.50 per sub already materializing.

Broadband SAC at $287 benefited from our fiber overbuild acceleration. In the U.S. Northeast and Midwest—where we've passed 8.2 million homes with 2 Gbps symmetrical speeds—door-to-door sales efficiency improved 11% via geo-fenced digital leads, outpacing Comcast Xfinity's bundle pricing wars. However, we saw a modest Q/Q uptick in the Southeast due to elevated installer incentives amid Hurricane Idalia recovery, adding ~$15 per sub. Wireline churn remains elite at 0.9% monthly, ensuring SAC payback in under 9 months at current $68 ARPU.

Our NovaStream DTC service, with 14.7 million subs (up 22% YoY), continues to lead on economics. SAC fell to $112 through addressable TV partnerships with Roku and Amazon Fire TV, where we pay only $8-10 per acquisition via shoppable ads—far below Netflix's reported $150+ blend. Content slate investments, like exclusive NFL Sunday Ticket streaming rights post our CBS deal, drove 40% of adds from cross-sells, with LTV now projecting $850 over 36 months versus $420 SAC cumulative.

Regionally, U.S. operations (85% of adds) saw SAC at $415, down 13% YoY, fueled by post-merger synergies from our 2022 AirWave acquisition, which expanded mid-band 5G coverage to 280 million POPS. In Europe—via our Vodafone JV in the UK and Germany—SAC rose 4% QoQ to €380 (~$410) due to aggressive 5G SA rollout subsidies amid regulatory spectrum auctions, but we're mitigating with eSIM self-provisioning, targeting 20% SAC relief by Q1 2025. APAC, our growth engine at 15% of adds, held SAC flat at A$520 (~$350 USD) despite competitive intensity from Singtel and Telstra; our Indonesia towerco partnerships slashed capex-per-site by 25%, indirectly bolstering acquisition margins.

Strategically, these trends underscore our LTV:SAC ratio expansion to 2.8x (from 2.3x YoY), with wireless payback periods now at 14 months versus 18 months industry average per New Street Research benchmarks. We're not chasing vanity adds—our mix shifted to 72% postpaid (up from 65%), prioritizing $75+ ARPU lines. Looking forward, we guide FY24 blended SAC to $440-$450, trending toward $410-$420 in FY25 as AI-driven personalization scales (piloting with Adobe Sensei for 30% better targeting) and we lean into enterprise SASE bundles. Risks include potential Android device price hikes or ad market softness, but our $2.1 billion free cash flow provides ample dry powder for opportunistic buys like regional MVNOs.

This positions us for sustainable 4-6% revenue growth and 150-200 bps EBITDA margin expansion.

Lisa Patel: Thank you, Michael. I would like to provide an update on our network performance and expansion. We continue to enhance our 5G network, achieving wider coverage and faster speeds across mid-band and mmWave assets. Our network reliability remains high at 99.999%, and we are investing in advanced technologies like Open RAN and AI-optimized spectrum management to further improve performance. We are also focused on optimizing our network for emerging applications like IoT, edge computing, and low-latency media streaming, building on the spectral efficiency gains Michael highlighted.

David Kim: Thank you, Lisa. I'm excited to share our commercial achievements. We saw strong growth in subscriber additions, driven by our innovative product offerings like Ultra5G bundles and targeted marketing campaigns leveraging programmatic ads. Customer satisfaction remains a top priority, with Net Promoter Scores up 5 points to 62, and we are continuously working to improve the customer experience across all touchpoints—from self-install kits to AI chatbots. We are also focused on expanding our partnerships to offer bundled services, such as NovaBundle with streaming tiers, enhancing customer value and driving ARPU.
